articles/decluttering-vs-organizing.caption: Two different jobs, and the switch between them matters. Sort asked whether a thing deserved to stay.

articles/everyday-things-out-of-reach.alt: The Prime Zone. A woman stands at a kitchen cabinet with the wall marked into four horizontal reach bands against knee, hip and shoulder height.
articles/everyday-things-out-of-reach.caption: Your body already drew this map. The band between your hips and your shoulders, at the front of the shelf, is the only space in the room that costs you nothing to use.

articles/everything-needs-an-assigned-ho.alt: Every Keeper Needs One Home. One item, one home, no duplicates.
articles/everything-needs-an-assigned-ho.caption: Five keepers, five homes, and every one of them a single motion away. Notice that nothing here was bought and nothing was hidden.

articles/family-wont-put-things-back.alt: The Path of Least Resistance. We all follow the easiest path, so design the easy one.
articles/family-wont-put-things-back.caption: Nobody chooses the harder route while carrying groceries. This is not laziness, it is arithmetic, and it runs the same way in every home and for every person in it.

articles/how-long-does-it-take-to-organi.alt: A Real 15-Minute Reset. Six photographed moments of one reset, timed.
articles/how-long-does-it-take-to-organi.caption: This is what a reset actually looks like, run once through. Nobody deep-cleans anything.

articles/how-long-to-keep-a-maybe.alt: Choose a Fair Decide-By Date. Match the test window to the item's natural use cycle.
articles/how-long-to-keep-a-maybe.caption: A fair deadline is one the item could actually be used within. Thirty days is cruel for a snow shovel and far too generous for a second can opener.

articles/how-to-organize-a-basement.alt: Five Common Home Zones. Five columns, each a zone named by its activity with a photograph and an includes checklist.
articles/how-to-organize-a-basement.caption: A few common zones cover most of a home. You will not need every one, and yours will have their own names.

articles/how-to-organize-a-junk-drawer.alt: Findability Feels Different. Two drawers photographed side by side.
articles/how-to-organize-a-junk-drawer.caption: Tidy and findable are not the same thing. Both of these drawers would pass a quick glance.

articles/how-to-organize-an-attic.alt: Daily, Weekly, Rare. Three columns of example items with the placement rule for each.
articles/how-to-organize-an-attic.caption: Three tiers, and the sorting takes about a minute per shelf. You do not need to be precise.

articles/is-that-really-a-backup.alt: The Duplicate Drawer. A kitchen drawer of many spatulas, whisks and turners, with a single spatula highlighted by a green check as the one that works: good condition, easy to use.
articles/is-that-really-a-backup.caption: Necessary includes a sensible quantity. The rest is surplus.

articles/more-storage-wont-fix-clutter.alt: Buy Storage Last. A shelf holding a labelled KEEP bin beside a basket marked DO NOT BUY YET and a checklist on a clipboard.
articles/more-storage-wont-fix-clutter.caption: Buy storage last, if at all. A bin bought before the pass simply gives the clutter a nicer place to live, and you will size it for the volume you had rather than the volume you are about to have.

articles/sentimental-items-without-guilt.alt: You Cannot Force a Maybe. Pressure creates guesses, patience creates evidence.
articles/sentimental-items-without-guilt.caption: Pressure does not create certainty. It creates a guess wearing the costume of a decision.

articles/tidy-is-not-the-same-as-safe.caption: The dangerous thing is rarely the ugly one. It is the ordinary object doing a second, quiet job you never gave it: the blanket that traps a foot, the blind cord within a child's reach, the tall set that can tip.

articles/what-is-6s.alt: 5S Becomes 6S. The top row shows the original five steps in order: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Standardize, Sustain.
articles/what-is-6s.caption: 5S, plus the one that protects people, equals 6S. Safety carries the number six because it was the last of the six to be named.

articles/what-is-a-micro-zone.alt: The Launch Pad Reveal. It was not six homes, it was always one zone.
articles/what-is-a-micro-zone.caption: The entryway was a zone all along.

articles/where-to-start-decluttering.alt: The First Target Map. High friction, low effort, start there.
articles/where-to-start-decluttering.caption: Two judgments, one decision. Score a space on friction, how often it costs you, and on effort, how big the job honestly is.

articles/why-5s-decays-after-six-months.alt: Finished Then Left versus Kept. The same living room shown across spring, summer, autumn, and winter, in two rows.
articles/why-5s-decays-after-six-months.caption: Held is not the same as kept. The top row is a home finished once and then left alone; season by season, life quietly fills it back up.

articles/why-a-shared-zone-never-stays-r.alt: Everyone's Job Is Nobody's Job. A split scene.
articles/why-a-shared-zone-never-stays-r.caption: A job that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. You met that line back in Shine, and it is even truer of a standard: leave it unowned and every person quietly assumes some other person has it handled.

articles/why-everyone-in-your-house-disa.alt: Tell versus Show. The same open kitchen cupboard shown twice.
articles/why-everyone-in-your-house-disa.caption: A written standard tells you what to do; a visual standard shows you what right looks like. On the left, a careful list still leaves her guessing what the shelf should actually look like.

articles/why-is-my-house-always-messy.alt: The Difference Between a Symptom and a Cause. Three columns, recurring symptoms, ask why, and underlying causes.
articles/why-is-my-house-always-messy.caption: Symptoms are what you see; causes are what you can change. The coats, the shoes, the dishes, the backpacks are not evidence that anyone is careless.

articles/why-it-lives-in-one-room-but-ge.alt: Store It Where You Use It. A before and after pair.
articles/why-it-lives-in-one-room-but-ge.caption: Store it where you use it, not where it belongs. Grouping all the coffee things with all the other pantry goods looks organised on a shelf and costs you a walk across the kitchen every single morning.

articles/why-mail-piles-up-by-the-door.caption: The out box is a staging post, not a verdict. It holds the things that belong somewhere else while you finish the pass, so that a single item does not send you walking to the far end of the house and back.

articles/why-the-medicine-cabinet-never-.caption: Give the dangerous things a home, and away becomes safe. The medicines, the batteries, the lighters, the knives, the cleaning bottles: each gets one protected place it goes back to every time.

articles/why-the-same-spot-never-gets-cl.alt: Cleaning Is Usually a Method Problem. You are not lazy, your method is.
articles/why-the-same-spot-never-gets-cl.caption: You do not have a cleaning problem. You have a method problem.

articles/why-you-always-lose-your-keys.alt: The Home Test. A home is good when putting it back is easier than putting it down.
articles/why-you-always-lose-your-keys.caption: This is the whole test, and it is decided in about a second. Both of these are technically "away".

articles/why-you-cant-find-the-right-cha.alt: The Hidden Cost of No Home. A thing without a home eventually claims someone else's.
articles/why-you-cant-find-the-right-cha.caption: A thing with nowhere to go does not stay still. It travels.

articles/why-you-cant-see-your-own-clutt.alt: Habituation. Your brain filters the familiar, cameras do not.
articles/why-you-cant-see-your-own-clutt.caption: This is not a character flaw. It is a feature of the brain.

articles/why-you-have-to-dig-for-what-yo.alt: The Reach Zone. The cabinet marked with three horizontal bands.
articles/why-you-have-to-dig-for-what-yo.caption: Every home has prime real estate. The band your hand finds without looking is the most valuable space you own, and most of us fill it with whatever happened to arrive first.

articles/why-you-keep-buying-things-you-.alt: The Glance Test. Two shelving units compared.
articles/why-you-keep-buying-things-you-.caption: The test is not whether the room looks organised. It is whether a stranger can use it.

articles/why-you-keep-running-out-of-thi.alt: Three Simple Visual Controls. Three numbered cards plus a bonus.
articles/why-you-keep-running-out-of-thi.caption: Almost every visual control in the house is one of these three, or a combination of them. A label names it, an outline places it, a boundary contains it.

articles/why-you-never-finish-a-zone.alt: The Power of the Timer. Two ways to face the same cleaning.
articles/why-you-never-finish-a-zone.caption: Set the timer, and stop when it rings. The timer is the whole trick, because a hard stop is what makes people willing to start.

articles/why-your-house-gets-messy-again.alt: The Saw-Tooth Pattern. Two line charts of clutter over a week, side by side.
articles/why-your-house-gets-messy-again.caption: A little, often, beats a rare heroic scrub every time, because the small easy pass actually happens. The red line is the house cleaned in dreaded weekend marathons; the green one is the house given a short reset most days.

articles/zone-too-small-for-what-it-hold.caption: Five jobs, or one. Asked to sort mail, hold keys, charge phones, catch homework, and display decor all at once, the space does none of them well.
